title: Weasel Words
objective: After this level you can spot vague words like "up to" and "helps" that make a claim sound bigger than it is.
summary: Weasel words like "up to" and "helps" make a claim sound big while promising almost nothing. Ask for the version you could check.

cards.headline: The sign shouts "70% OFF!" Squint, and there's a tiny "Up to".
cards.body: One logic textbook uses exactly this shop window. For all you know, one unloved item at the back is 70% off and everything else barely budges. Two small words turned a promise into a ceiling.

cards.headline: Why weasels?
cards.body: Merriam-Webster defines a weasel word as one used to evade a direct statement. The name comes from old lore that a weasel could suck out an egg and leave the shell intact: it looks fine but it's empty. Real weasels can't manage it. Weasel words can. The term's first known use was in 1900.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the date. Remember the egg: a weasel word looks full and holds nothing.

cards.headline: "Up to" on trial
cards.body: In 2012 the US Federal Trade Commission released a study of ads for replacement windows promising "up to 47%" savings on energy costs. Many consumers believed they would get the full 47%. The FTC's view: if you say "up to", you should be able to show people are likely to get that result under normal conditions.

cards.headline: Make it checkable
cards.body: Other weasels are quieter. "Helps fight plaque" dodges a direct statement: it doesn't say how much, for whom or compared with what, so almost no result could prove it wrong. The fix is to ask for the version you could check. How much? For whom? By when? A claim that can't lose can't tell you much either.

cards.headline: Weasel words: caught
learned: Weasel words dodge a direct statement
"Up to" promises a ceiling, not a result
Many readers take "up to" as the maximum they'll get
Ask: how much, for whom, by when?

questions.prompt: Match each piece of the weasel word lesson with its partner on the cards.

pairs.right: Used to evade a direct statement

questions.explanation: A weasel word is one used to evade a direct statement. Old lore said a weasel could suck out an egg and leave the shell. The Federal Trade Commission studied ads promising "up to 47%" savings.

questions.prompt: How did the "up to 47%" window ads mislead, according to the FTC's 2012 study?

options.label: The windows raised energy costs instead
options.rationale: The study was about what buyers believed, not results.

options.label: The ads hid the price of the windows
Many buyers expected the full 47% savings
Nobody noticed the savings claim at all
options.rationale: People noticed it and read it as the maximum.

questions.explanation: "Up to" sets a ceiling, but many consumers read it as the result they'd get.

questions.prompt: Level 4 says a factual claim can be checked by observation or research. Which ad line would be easiest to check?

options.label: Helps fight plaque
options.rationale: "Helps" doesn't say how much, so almost nothing could disprove it.

questions.explanation: It says how much and by when, so observation could show it true or false.
